questions.stem: In the gold foil experiment by Rutherford's team, almost all of the alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did this show?
options: The positive charge is spread through the atom
Most of the volume of an atom is empty space
Gold atoms carry no electric charge at all
Alpha particles are too small to hit atoms
questions.explanation: If most alpha particles meet nothing that deflects them, the atom must be mostly empty. The rare large deflections showed that the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny central nucleus, not spread through the atom.

questions.stem: Which equation correctly shows what happens inside a nucleus during beta-minus decay?
options: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino
p → n + e⁻ + neutrino
n → p + e⁺ + neutrino
p → n + e⁺ + antineutrino
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino. Charge is conserved: 0 = +1 − 1. In beta-plus decay a proton becomes a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino.

questions.stem: Fluorine-18 (Z = 9), used in medical imaging, decays by positron emission. Which equation is correct?
options: ¹⁸F → ¹⁸O + e⁺ + neutrino, with oxygen Z = 8
¹⁸F → ¹⁸Ne + e⁺ + neutrino, with neon Z = 10
¹⁸F → ¹⁸O + e⁻ + antineutrino, with oxygen Z = 8
¹⁸F → ¹⁴N + e⁺ + neutrino, with nitrogen Z = 7
questions.explanation: A proton becomes a neutron, so Z falls by one, from 9 to 8 (oxygen), while the mass number stays 18. The positron is accompanied by a neutrino. Z rising by one would be beta-minus decay.

questions.stem: Why did physicists propose that a neutrino, or antineutrino, is emitted in beta decay?
options: The beta particles were too heavy to be electrons, so another particle had to share their mass
The daughter nucleus had the wrong charge, so another charged particle had to be emitted
The beta particles all had the same energy, so another particle had to explain their speed
The beta particles had a range of energies, so another particle had to carry the missing energy
questions.explanation: If only an electron and a daughter nucleus were produced, every beta particle from a given decay would have the same energy. Instead they show a continuous spread, so a nearly massless, neutral particle must take the rest of the energy and momentum.

questions.stem: Cobalt-60 (Z = 27) undergoes beta-minus decay to nickel-60, and the excited nickel nucleus then emits gamma rays. Which set of products is correct?
options: Nickel-60 (Z = 28), an electron, an antineutrino and gamma photons
Nickel-60 (Z = 26), a positron, a neutrino and gamma photons
Nickel-56 (Z = 28), an alpha particle and gamma photons only
Nickel-60 (Z = 28), an electron and a neutron, with no photons
questions.explanation: Beta-minus decay raises Z by one, from 27 to 28, with A unchanged at 60, and emits an electron and an antineutrino. The daughter is left in an excited state and drops to its ground state by emitting gamma rays.

questions.stem: After an alpha or beta decay, why is gamma radiation often emitted as well?
options: The electrons around the daughter nucleus fall into the nucleus and release energy
The parent nucleus emits a gamma ray just before it decays, to signal the decay
The daughter nucleus is left in an excited state and releases energy as a photon
The emitted alpha or beta particle turns into a gamma ray after travelling a short way
questions.explanation: The daughter nucleus often forms with excess energy. It drops to a lower nuclear energy level by emitting a gamma photon, which changes neither A nor Z.

questions.stem: What is a radioactive decay series?
options: A graph of activity against time for a sample containing a single isotope
A chain of decays from a parent nucleus through radioactive daughters to a stable nucleus
A list of isotopes of one element arranged in order of increasing half-life
A set of fission reactions, each started by neutrons from the one before
questions.explanation: Many heavy nuclei decay into daughters that are themselves radioactive, and so on, by alpha and beta decays, until a stable nucleus such as lead-206 is reached. Neutron-triggered fissions form a chain reaction, which is different.

questions.stem: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays through a series of alpha and beta-minus decays to stable lead-206 (Z = 82). How many of each decay occur?
options: 10 alpha and 2 beta-minus
8 alpha and 6 beta-minus
8 alpha and 10 beta-minus
6 alpha and 8 beta-minus
questions.explanation: Only alpha decay changes A, by 4 each time: (238 − 206)/4 = 8 alphas. These lower Z by 16, to 76, but lead has Z = 82, so 6 beta-minus decays must each raise Z by one. Assuming every decay lowers Z gives 10 betas.

questions.stem: Thorium-232 (Z = 90) decays through a series to stable lead-208 (Z = 82). How many alpha and beta-minus decays occur?
options: 6 alpha and 8 beta-minus
4 alpha and 6 beta-minus
8 alpha and 2 beta-minus
6 alpha and 4 beta-minus
questions.explanation: (232 − 208)/4 = 6 alpha decays, which would lower Z by 12, to 78. To reach Z = 82, four beta-minus decays must each raise Z by one.

questions.stem: What does an activity of 1 becquerel mean?
options: One nucleus decays each second
One gram of the isotope decays each second
Half of the nuclei decay in one second
One decay is detected each minute
questions.explanation: Activity is the number of nuclei decaying per second, and 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. A detector usually records only a fraction of the decays, so a count rate is not the same as the activity.

questions.stem: A radioisotope has a half-life of 30 s. What is its decay constant?
options: 43 s⁻¹
21 s⁻¹
questions.explanation: λ = 0.693/T½ = 0.693/30 = 0.023 s⁻¹. 0.033 s⁻¹ is 1/T½, which leaves out the factor of ln 2 = 0.693.

questions.stem: A sample contains 2.0 × 10¹⁰ nuclei of iodine-131, which has a half-life of 8.0 days. What is the activity of the sample?
options: 2.0 × 10¹⁰ Bq
questions.explanation: Convert the half-life to seconds: 8.0 × 86 400 = 6.91 × 10⁵ s. λ = 0.693/6.91 × 10⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹, and A = λN = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.0 × 10¹⁰ = 2.0 × 10⁴ Bq. Leaving λ in day⁻¹ gives 1.7 × 10⁹, which is decays per day, not per second.

questions.stem: An isotope has a half-life of 4.0 hours. What fraction of the original nuclei remains after 10 hours?
questions.explanation: N/N₀ = 2^(−t/T½) = 2^(−10/4.0) = 2^(−2.5) = 0.18. The time is not a whole number of half-lives, so the answer lies between ¼ after 8 h and ⅛ after 12 h.

questions.stem: A source has an initial activity of 500 Bq and a decay constant of 0.10 h⁻¹. What is its activity after 5.0 hours?
options: 303 Bq
250 Bq
450 Bq
questions.explanation: A = A₀e^(−λt) = 500 × e^(−0.50) = 303 Bq. 250 Bq would require 5.0 h to be a half-life, but the half-life here is 0.693/0.10 = 6.9 h.

questions.stem: Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years. How long does it take for the activity of a cobalt-60 source to fall to 20% of its initial value?
options: 26.4 years
21.1 years
1.70 years
12.2 years
questions.explanation: 0.20 = 2^(−t/5.27), so t/5.27 = log₂5 = 2.32 and t = 12.2 years. Falling to 20% takes between two half-lives, 25%, and three half-lives, 12.5%. Dividing 100% by 20% and multiplying by the half-life gives 26.4 years.

questions.stem: The atomic mass unit, or dalton, is defined as:
options: the mass of a single hydrogen-1 atom
the mass of one proton plus one neutron
one sixteenth of the mass of an oxygen-16 atom
one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
questions.explanation: 1 u is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, about 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Protons, neutrons and hydrogen atoms each have masses slightly above 1 u.

questions.stem: The masses of a proton, a neutron and a deuteron (²H nucleus) are 1.67262 × 10⁻²⁷, 1.67493 × 10⁻²⁷ and 3.34358 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. What is the binding energy of the deuteron? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The mass defect is 1.67262 + 1.67493 − 3.34358 = 0.00397 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 3.97 × 10⁻³⁰ kg. E = Δmc² = 3.97 × 10⁻³⁰ × 9.00 × 10¹⁶ = 3.57 × 10⁻¹³ J, about 2.2 MeV. Multiplying by c instead of c² gives 1.19 × 10⁻²¹ J.

questions.stem: A helium-4 nucleus has a binding energy of 28.3 MeV. What is its binding energy per nucleon?
options: 14.2 MeV
113 MeV
3.54 MeV
7.08 MeV
questions.explanation: Helium-4 has 4 nucleons, so 28.3/4 = 7.08 MeV per nucleon. Dividing by its 2 protons only gives 14.2 MeV.

questions.stem: Which nucleus is the most stable?
options: The one with the greatest number of protons in its nucleus
The one with the smallest binding energy per nucleon
The one with the greatest binding energy per nucleon
The one with the greatest total mass in atomic mass units
questions.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon measures how tightly each nucleon is held, on average. The higher it is, the more energy is needed to pull the nucleus apart. Total binding energy is larger for big nuclei, but they are less tightly bound per nucleon.

questions.stem: Radium-226 decays by alpha emission to radon-222. The atomic masses are radium-226 226.025410 u, radon-222 222.017578 u and helium-4 4.002603 u, and 1 u = 931.5 MeV. How much energy is released?
options: 4.87 MeV
3729 MeV
8.73 MeV
questions.explanation: The mass decrease is 226.025410 − (222.017578 + 4.002603) = 0.005229 u. The energy released is 0.005229 × 931.5 = 4.87 MeV, shared as kinetic energy, mostly by the alpha particle. 0.00523 is the mass change in u, not an energy.

questions.stem: In one fission of a uranium-235 nucleus, the total mass of the products is about 0.20 u less than that of the reactants. Taking 1 u = 931.5 MeV, about how much energy is released?
options: 0.20 MeV
4700 MeV
93 MeV
190 MeV
questions.explanation: By E = mc², the lost mass appears as energy: 0.20 × 931.5 = 186 MeV, about 190 MeV, mostly as kinetic energy of the fission fragments. Mass-energy is conserved, even though mass alone is not.

questions.stem: On which particles does the strong nuclear force act?
options: Protons and neutrons, but not electrons
Protons and electrons, but not neutrons
Electrons only, holding them in orbit
All charged particles, but not neutrons
questions.explanation: The strong force acts between nucleons, protons and neutrons, which is why it holds the nucleus together. Electrons do not feel it. It acts on neutrons, which have no charge, so it is not an electrical force.

questions.stem: In nuclear fission, what is meant by the critical mass of a fissile material?
options: The mass of fuel used up in a reactor before it must be replaced
The mass of a single uranium nucleus at the moment it undergoes fission
The smallest mass in which, on average, each fission causes at least one more fission
The largest mass that can be stored safely before it explodes without any neutrons
questions.explanation: In a small piece of fuel, too many neutrons escape through the surface before causing fission, so the chain reaction dies out. Above the critical mass, enough neutrons are captured to keep the chain reaction going.

questions.stem: In a fission power station, what does the heat exchanger do?
options: It slows down fast neutrons so that they are more likely to cause further fissions
It absorbs extra neutrons so that the chain reaction does not run out of control
It converts the kinetic energy of the fission fragments directly into electrical energy
It transfers heat from the coolant that passed through the core to separate water, making steam
questions.explanation: The coolant carries heat from the core to the heat exchanger, where it boils water in a separate circuit. The steam drives turbines connected to generators. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job, and absorbing them is the job of the control rods.

questions.stem: In the Standard Model, protons and neutrons are made of up and down quarks. Which quarks make up a proton?
options: Two up quarks and one down quark
One up quark and two down quarks
Three up quarks
One up quark and one down quark
questions.explanation: A proton is uud. With up quarks of charge +2/3 and down quarks of −1/3, the total is +2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1. The neutron is udd.

questions.stem: A neutron is made of one up quark (+2/3) and two down quarks (−1/3 each). What is its total charge?
questions.explanation: +2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0, so the neutron is neutral. Two up quarks and one down quark would give +1, the proton's charge.

questions.stem: In the Standard Model, what holds the quarks inside a proton together?
options: The strong force, carried by gluons acting on the quarks' colour charge
The electromagnetic force, carried by photons acting on the quarks' electric charge
The weak force, carried by W and Z bosons acting on the quarks' mass
Gravity, which is strong enough at very short distances to bind the quarks
questions.explanation: Quarks carry a property called colour charge, and the strong force between them is carried by gluons. Electrical forces alone would push the two up quarks in a proton apart.

questions.stem: Which statement about colour charge in protons and neutrons is correct?
options: Colour charge describes the colour of light that quarks emit when a nucleon is excited
Colour charge is the same as electric charge, so the proton has colour and the neutron does not
Each nucleon contains three quarks of different colour charges, so it is colour neutral overall
Each nucleon contains three quarks of the same colour charge, so it has a net colour
questions.explanation: Colour charge comes in three types, called red, green and blue, which have nothing to do with visible colour. Each proton and neutron contains one quark of each colour, so it is colour neutral overall.
